t.5.12.2: But that great monkey, standing upon the rampart, his whole body thrilled with joy, beheld trees of many kinds with blossoming tops, as at the beginning of spring.
t.5.12.1: Having reflected for what seemed a moment and having grasped her in his mind, he, of great splendour, leapt onto the rampart of that dwelling.
t.5.12.4: Then, like an iron arrow loosed from the bowstring, he leapt into the grove of trees, covered with mango woods and enveloped by hundreds of creepers.
t.5.12.3: He saw sāla trees, aśokas, bhavyas and campakas in full bloom, uddālakas, nāgavṛkṣas, mango trees, and kapimukhas too.
t.5.12.5: He entered that wondrous place, resounding with birds and surrounded on every side by trees of silver and of gold.
t.5.12.6: The monkey Hanumān beheld it, variegated with birds and herds of deer, rich in wondrous woods, and shining like the newly risen sun.
t.5.12.7: He saw the grove surrounded by trees of many kinds laden with flowers and fruits, and ever frequented by intoxicated cuckoos and great black bees.
t.5.12.8: At a time when men were joyful and the season teemed with beasts and birds, she resounded with the cries of impassioned peacocks and was filled with flocks of many kinds of birds.
t.5.12.9: Searching for the faultless princess with the beautiful hips, the monkey woke the birds that had been sleeping peacefully.
t.5.12.10: Struck by the wings of flocks of birds flying up, the sāla trees released showers of flowers, many-coloured and of every kind.
t.5.12.11: Strewn all over with flowers, Hanumān, the son of Māruta, shone in the midst of the Aśoka grove like a mountain made of flowers.
t.5.12.12: Seeing the monkey rushing toward all the directions and moving among the clusters of trees, all beings thought he was Vasanta, the spring itself.
t.5.12.13: Strewn with flowers of many kinds that had fallen from the trees, the earth there shone like a young woman adorned with ornaments.
t.5.12.14: Then those trees, violently shaken by the mighty monkey, shed their many-coloured blossoms.
t.5.12.16: Shaken by the swift Hanūmān, those excellent trees, rich in blossoms, quickly shed their flowers, leaves and fruits.
t.5.12.15: The trees, their crowns stripped of leaves by the shaking, their flowers and fruits scattered and fallen, looked like defeated gamblers who have had to lay down their clothes and ornaments.
t.5.12.17: Bereft of their flocks of birds and left with only their trunks to stand upon, all those trees became as though shaken bare by the wind.
t.5.12.18: It was like a young woman with tossed and dishevelled hair, her cosmetic paint smudged, her lovely teeth and lips drunk deep with kisses, and her body marked by nails and teeth.
t.5.12.19: Thus crushed by his tail and hands and by his two feet, the Aśoka grove came to have its finest trees broken down.
t.5.12.20: The monkey forcefully scattered the garlands of great creepers, as the wind in the rainy season scatters the masses of clouds on the Vindhya.
t.5.12.21: Roaming there, the monkey saw delightful floors of gems and of silver, and likewise floors of gold.
t.5.12.22: And here and there he saw ponds of many different shapes, filled with the finest water and furnished with steps of costly gems.
t.5.12.23: Their inner floors were paved with pearls, coral, sand and crystal, and they were adorned with wondrous golden trees growing along their banks.
t.5.12.25: On every side they were adorned with long, auspicious rivers lined with trees, whose waters were like nectar.
t.5.12.24: They were thick with clusters of full-blown lotuses and water-lilies, echoing with the calls of cakravākas, resounding with the cries of gallinules, and ringing with the voices of haṃsas and sārasa cranes.
t.5.12.26: They were overspread with hundreds of creepers and covered all around with saṃtānaka trees; their woods were enclosed by thickets of many kinds, and the spaces between were filled with karavīra shrubs.
t.5.12.27: Then he saw a mountain resembling a rain-cloud, with towering summits and wondrous peaks, surrounded on every side by other peaks.
t.5.12.28: The tiger among monkeys saw a lovely mountain in the world, spread with rock-houses and covered all over with many kinds of trees.
t.5.12.29: And the monkey saw a river falling down from that mountain, like a beloved woman who, springing up from the lap of her beloved, has fallen away.
t.5.12.30: It was adorned with trees whose tips had fallen into the water, like an angry young woman being held back by her dear kinsmen.
t.5.12.31: And the great monkey saw her again, her waters turned back, like a beloved woman who, appeased, had come back once more to her lover.
t.5.12.33: He saw also an artificial oblong pond, filled with cool water, with steps made of the finest gems and adorned with sands of pearl.
t.5.12.32: Not far from it, Hanumān, the tiger among monkeys, the son of Māruta, saw lotus ponds teeming with flocks of many kinds of birds.
t.5.12.34: It was wondrous with diverse herds of animals and had colourful groves, and it was adorned on every side with very great palaces built by Viśvakarman and with artificial groves as well.
t.5.12.35: Whatever trees stood there, laden with flowers and bearing fruit, all had canopies and raised terraces, and all were encircled by golden platforms.
t.5.12.36: That great monkey saw a single golden śiṃśapā tree, covered with many spreading creepers and with many leaves.
t.5.12.37: He saw stretches of ground and springs flowing in hollows, and he beheld other trees of gold that shone like fire.
t.5.12.38: By the radiance of those trees, as if by the radiance of Meru, the great monkey, the heroic vānara, then thought, "I am golden."
t.5.12.39: Seeing it fanned by clusters of golden trees and by the wind, and resounding with the tinkling of hundreds of little bells, he was filled with wonder.
t.5.12.41: Here I shall see Vaidehī, longing for the sight of Rāma, afflicted with sorrow, wandering by chance hither and thither.
t.5.12.40: Having climbed that lovely śiṃśapā tree, its crown in full bloom, bearing tender shoots and young leaves and thickly covered with foliage, the one of great speed…
t.5.12.42: And this Aśoka grove of the evil-minded one is exceedingly delightful, adorned with campaka trees, sandalwood trees, and bakula trees as well.
t.5.12.43: And here is this lovely lotus pond, frequented by flocks of birds; surely Jānakī, the queen of Rāma, will come to it.
t.5.12.45: Or else that fawn-eyed lady, well acquainted with this grove and worn thin with longing for Rāma, will come here into the grove.
t.5.12.44: That lovely lady, Rāma's chief queen, ever dear to Rāghava, Jānakī, who is skilled in wandering through forests, will surely come.
t.5.12.46: That lovely-eyed queen, tormented by grief for Rāma, who has always delighted in dwelling in the forest and roaming the woods, will surely come here.
t.5.12.47: Surely, in former days, the beloved wife of Rāma, the virtuous daughter of Janaka, constantly longed for the creatures that roam the forest.
t.5.12.48: Surely Jānakī, the youthful lady of lovely complexion, her mind intent on the hour of twilight, will come to this river of auspicious waters for the sake of her twilight worship.
t.5.12.49: And this beautiful Aśoka grove is fitting for her too, the lovely one who is the wife of Rāma, lord of kings, and his equal.
t.5.12.50: If that queen whose face is like the moon, lord of the stars, is still alive, she will surely come to this river of auspicious waters.
t.5.12.51: Having thus resolved, the great-souled Hanumān, hidden in a richly blossoming tree dense with leaves, waited for the wife of the lord of men, and, keeping watch, observed everything.
